summary: Suggests changing how IP addresses are specified by adding new classes of networks, called F, G, H, and K, to reduce wasted address space and make more addresses available. It is an informational idea paper.

plainLanguage.summary: Addresses came in only a few sizes, and many were wasted. This paper suggests adding more sizes so fewer are thrown away.

questions: ip address class f g h k
new ip address classes f g h k
why not implement new address classes
subtitle: Adding smaller IP address sizes to reduce waste

tldr.problem: Class A, B, and C IP addresses came in three fixed sizes. Organizations needing only a few addresses had to take a Class C with room for 254 addresses, wasting hundreds. This granularity problem would worsen as the Internet grew.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes adding four new address classes (F, G, H, K) by subdividing the unused Class C space. Each new class supports different minimum sizes: from 15 addresses (Class F) down to 2 (Class K), allowing organizations to request only what they need.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was never adopted. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) and later IPv6 solved the address space problem more comprehensively, making this incremental approach obsolete.

today: RFC 1375's proposal was never implemented. In 1993, RFC 1519 introduced CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing), which made fixed address classes obsolete by allowing any prefix length. Later, IPv6 with its 128-bit addresses rendered the address exhaustion problem moot. This RFC is an archive of one path not taken, but it correctly identified a real problem that the Internet community solved through different means.

sections.title: The Address Granularity Problem
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, IP addresses were 32-bit numbers allocated in three main classes: A, B, and C. A Class A network supported over 16 million local addresses. Class B supported about 65,000. Class C supported 254. There was no way to request something smaller.

This created waste. A small organization or community bulletin board that needed only 4 or 5 IP addresses had to request a Class C network, wasting over 240 addresses. As the RFC notes, the smallest possible allocation allowed for up to 254 addresses, so any request smaller than that meant waste. With growing demand—more businesses, more devices, cheaper connections—this inefficiency would become severe.

The RFC author foresaw a future where small organizations, non-computer devices (like printers or fax machines), and even consumer computer bulletin boards might want Internet connectivity. All of them would eat up Class C space, exacerbating address shortage. The proposal is to create intermediate address classes that fit small deployments better.
sections.plainLanguage: In the 1990s, Internet addresses came in only three sizes. If you needed a small address block, you had to take a big one and throw away most of it. This paper suggests making smaller sizes.

sections.title: The New Address Classes
sections.content:
The proposal modifies the original Class C definition and adds four new classes, all using the address space that would have been Class C under the old scheme.

Class C (revised) changes from a 3-bit prefix (110) to a 4-bit prefix (1100), reducing the number of Class C networks from 2,097,152 to 1,048,576, but freeing address space for new classes. Class F addresses begin with 5 bits (11010) and support 1 to 15 local addresses per network, allowing 16,777,256 Class F networks. Class G begins with 6 bits (110110) and is reserved for future use. Class H addresses begin with 7 bits (1101110) and support 1 to 7 local addresses, allowing 4,194,304 Class H networks. Class K addresses begin with 7 bits (1101111) and support only 1 or 2 local addresses, allowing 33,554,432 Class K networks.

The RFC includes bit diagrams for each address format showing where the prefix ends and the local address space begins. It notes that addresses can still be written in dotted decimal form (n.n.n.n), but routers and bridges must not assume the last 8 bits alone identify the local part—new classes use fewer bits for local addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of just one size of small network, the plan offers four sizes: tiny (K), very small (H), small (F), and regular (C). Each one wastes less space.

sections.title: Address Assignment and Routing
sections.content:
The RFC suggests that the new classes could optionally be assigned by geographic region, similar to international telephone dialing. For example, bits 5–8 in a Class F address, bits 7–10 in Class H, and bits 6–9 in Class K could encode the world region, making routing decisions easier. The RFC sketches a mapping similar to ITU phone zones (1 for North America, 8 for Asia) but notes that true geographic routing is not necessary—shortest-path routing based on network reachability would work fine.

Organizations needing only a few addresses could apply for multiple contiguous blocks of the appropriate class. For instance, a site needing 20 addresses might request multiple Class F blocks instead of wasting a Class C.

The RFC emphasizes that the new classes occupy space not yet allocated, so no existing allocations would be disrupted. The proposal is purely about reserving and using previously unused address space more efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: New address blocks could be assigned with hints about where in the world they are, making routing easier. Or you could just ask for multiple small blocks if one is not enough.

sections.title: Impact and Adoption
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges a deeper problem: the possibility of eventually running out of IP address space entirely. It debates two futures: either the Internet backbone becomes a public utility paid for by taxes or other means, or it becomes fully commercialized. In either case, demand for addresses would skyrocket.

The proposal is pragmatic: take some unused Class C space and reserve it for these new classes. Since Class C already occupies far less space than Class A or B, and much of it remains unallocated, this move would not cause disruption. Organizations unable to get traditional Class C addresses could instead use the new, smaller classes.

However, the RFC notes that implementation requires bridges, routers, and other infrastructure to stop assuming that only the last 8 bits identify local addresses. This architectural change, while not enormous, meant cooperation across many vendors and systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is not a perfect fix for address shortage, but it helps. It uses space that was not being used anyway, so it would not hurt existing networks.
